concept.title: Quantum Random Walks on Cayley Graphs: Spectral Gaps and Mixing Times
concept.concept_description: A quantum random walk on a group G is defined by a unitary operator U = sum_{g in S} |g><0| (where S is a generating set) acting on the Hilbert space l^2(G). The walk is periodic if U^k = I for some k, and mixing if the probability distribution P_n(g) = |<g|U^n|0>|^2 converges to the uniform distribution on G. Conjecture: for the Cayley graph Cay(G, S) where G is a finite group and S is a symmetric generating set, the quantum walk mixes in O(sqrt(|G|) * log(|G|)) steps, which is quadratically faster than the classical random walk (which takes O(|G|^2) steps for the spectral gap to kick in). The mixing time is determined by the spectral gap of U: tau_mix ~ 1/gap where gap = 1 - |lambda_2| and lambda_2 is the second-largest eigenvalue of U. Conjecture: for Cay(G, S) with S = the set of transpositions in S_n, the spectral gap of U is Omega(1/n), giving a mixing time of O(n * log(n)). This matches the known classical mixing time of O(n * log(n)) for the random transposition walk on S_n. The quantum advantage comes from the quadratically faster convergence of the probability distribution, not from the spectral gap. Test: simulate quantum random walks on Cayley graphs of S_n, S_n, A_5, and Z_n, measure the mixing time, and verify tau_mix = O(sqrt(|G|) * log(|G|)). Impact: quantum random walks mix quadratically faster than classical random walks on Cayley graphs. The quadratic speedup is universal.

# Future Directions: complex-weighted undirected random graphs

This cycle deepened the theory of the fixed-amplitude model, where every present edge
of an undirected graph carries a single common complex weight `z`.  The central new
result is *spectral line-locking*: for a symmetric edge relation and nonzero `z`,
every eigenvalue of the weighted adjacency matrix is `z` times a real number, so the
entire spectrum collapses onto the one-dimensional line `ℝ·z`.  We also established
the global multiplicative invariants (determinant scales by `zⁿ`, loopless trace
vanishes) and showed that the complete-graph mean-direction eigenvalue `(n-1)z`
escapes the naive radius `√n·‖z‖` for every order `n ≥ 3`.  These findings suggest
the following bold, testable conjectures.

## 1. Two-dimensional spectra require broken phase symmetry

**Conjecture.** If the edges of a random graph carry *independent* complex phases
(each present edge `(i,j)` weighted by an independent unit-modulus random variable,
with `w_{ji} = \overline{w_{ij}}` relaxed to genuine independence), then the empirical
spectral distribution of the normalized adjacency matrix converges, as `n → ∞`, to a
rotationally invariant law supported on a full two-dimensional disk — in sharp
contrast to the line-locked fixed-amplitude model.

The key insight is that line-locking is caused entirely by the scalar–Hermitian
factorization `z·B`: all randomness sits inside a single Hermitian matrix, and one
complex scalar can only rotate and dilate a real spectrum. Breaking the shared phase
is therefore both necessary and, conjecturally, sufficient to recover circular-law
behaviour.

Why now? The exact obstruction has been isolated in closed form, so the search for a
circular law can be aimed precisely at the models that violate the factorization,
rather than at the undirected fixed-amplitude model where no such law can exist.

## 2. A phase-transition threshold for the mean-direction outlier

**Conjecture.** For the fixed-amplitude Erdős–Rényi model `G(n, p)` with weight `z`,
there is a sharp threshold `p*(n)` such that above it the largest-modulus eigenvalue
is asymptotically `p·(n-1)·|z|` (the mean-direction outlier), while the bulk stays
within radius `2√{np(1-p)}·|z|`; the outlier separates from the bulk exactly when
`p·(n-1) > 2√{np(1-p)}`.

The key insight is that the deterministic complete-graph computation `(n-1)z` is the
`p → 1` endpoint of a family of expected row sums `p·(n-1)`, and the outlier/bulk
separation is governed by comparing this expected row sum with the semicircle radius
of the centered indicator matrix.

Why now? Both endpoints are already understood — the deterministic outlier for the
complete graph and the row-sum disk bound scaled by `|z|` — so the remaining task is
to interpolate them across `p`, a concrete and falsifiable analytic problem.

## 3. Reality of Rayleigh quotients characterizes the line-locked class

**Conjecture.** Among all weighting schemes assigning a complex number to each edge of
a fixed graph, the weighted adjacency matrix has its full spectrum confined to a
single complex line through the origin *if and only if* the scheme is a complex
scalar multiple of a Hermitian matrix; equivalently, if and only if the Rayleigh
quotient `⟨v, A v⟩` is a fixed complex multiple of a real number for all `v`.

The key insight is that reality of the Hermitian Rayleigh quotient is exactly what
pins each eigenvalue to the line, so the converse should hold: line confinement of
the whole spectrum forces the matrix back into the scalar-Hermitian class.

Why now? The forward direction is now established in full, and its proof is entirely
Rayleigh-quotient based, which hands over the precise algebraic invariant whose
converse can be attacked directly.

## 4. Determinant zeros track the underlying combinatorics

**Conjecture.** The weighted determinant `det(z·B) = zⁿ·det(B)` vanishes for a fixed
nonzero `z` if and only if the underlying graph has no perfect matching of a certain
signed type; consequently, for random `G(n, p)` the probability that the weighted
matrix is singular exhibits the same threshold as the appearance of an isolated
vertex, independent of `z`.

The key insight is that the complex amplitude is a global unit that cannot create or
destroy singularity — singularity is a purely combinatorial property of the indicator
matrix `B`, so all `z`-dependence factors out through `zⁿ`.

Why now? The clean determinant factorization makes the `z`-independence of singularity
explicit, reducing a question about complex-weighted matrices to a classical question
about zero-one matrices with known threshold behaviour.

# Computational Evidence — Transfinite Cellular Automata on ω²

This note records the finite-case sanity checks behind the formal results in
`Catalog/Applications/OrdinalCellularAutomata/TransfiniteComputation.lean`.

## Setup

A computation of order type `ω²` is indexed by pairs `(block, tick) : ℕ × ℕ`
under lexicographic order. Successor ticks apply the Rule 110 local update
`rule110Step`; the start of each new block is chosen by a *limit rule* that may
read the entire preceding `ω`-history.

For the scheduled family we use `predicateLimit P`, which at the boundary
following block `k` writes the single bit `P k` into cell `0` and clears every
other cell.

## Small-case calculations

Successor evolution reduces to ordinary iteration `rule110Step^[n]`:

- Block 0, tick n: `rule110Step^[n] initial`.
- All-zero tape is a Rule 110 fixed point:
  `rule110Step (fun _ => false) = fun _ => false`
  (checked cell-by-cell for positions `0`, `1`, `≥2`; formalised as an `example`).

Boundary bits for the schedule `P n = decide (Even n)`:

| block k | boundary cell value `scheduledOmegaRun P initial (k+1) 0 0` |
|--------:|:----------------------------------------------------------|
| 0       | `Even 0 = true`                                           |
| 1       | `Even 1 = false`                                          |
| 2       | `Even 2 = true`                                           |
| 3       | `Even 3 = false`                                          |
| 4       | `Even 4 = true`                                           |

The block-4 entry (`= true`) is recorded as an `example` in the file via
`scheduledOmegaRun_boundary`.

General identity checked at blocks 0, 1, 5:
`scheduledOmegaRun P initial (k+1) 0 0 = P k` (theorem `scheduledOmegaRun_boundary`).

## Counterexample hunt

The universal claim under test is *faithfulness*: distinct schedules produce
distinct histories. On the finite window "read cell 0 at each boundary" this is
just `boundaryTrace ∘ scheduledOmegaRun = id`, and the diagonal test

`d n = if enumerate n n then false else true`

defeats any proposed enumeration `enumerate : ℕ → (ℕ → Bool)` (theorem
`no_predicate_enumeration`), so no countable list of histories can be complete
(`no_history_enumeration`). No counterexample to faithfulness was found; on the
contrary it upgrades to an exact cardinality: the histories realise the full
continuum (`continuum_scheduled_histories`).

## OEIS

No integer sequence drives the construction; target selection used no external
sequence signal, so no OEIS/LMFDB object was consulted.

## Conclusion

The finite checks are consistent with, and are subsumed by, the formal theorems:
successor locality, boundary faithfulness, non-enumerability via diagonalisation,
and the continuum-cardinality bridge.

## Current state

`Catalog/Applications/OrdinalCellularAutomata/TransfiniteComputation.lean`
develops a two-layer semantics for cellular dynamics indexed by the order type
`ω²` (pairs `(block, tick)` in lexicographic order):

- **Successor layer.** An arbitrary state transition system supplies the
  successor update; Rule 110 (`rule110Step`) is the concrete instance, and it is
  shown to remain radius-one local at transfinite times (`rule110Step_local`).
- **Limit layer.** A history functional selects the state at each block
  boundary. `predicateLimit` writes a chosen Boolean bit at cell 0.

Key theorems (all `sorry`-free, axioms limited to `propext`, `Classical.choice`,
`Quot.sound`):

- `omegaSquaredRun_succ`, `omegaSquaredRun_limit`, `omegaSquaredRun_eq_iterate` —
  structural laws of the transfinite run.
- `scheduledOmegaRun_boundary`, `boundaryTrace_scheduled` — boundary read-out is
  faithful to the schedule.
- `scheduledOmegaRun_injective` — distinct schedules give distinct histories.
- `no_predicate_enumeration`, `no_history_enumeration` — Cantor diagonalisation:
  neither Boolean predicates nor transfinite histories are countably enumerable.
- `continuum_scheduled_histories` — **cross-domain bridge**: the space of
  scheduled Rule 110 histories has cardinality exactly `𝔠 = 2^{ℵ₀}`, tying
  symbolic dynamics / ordinal recursion to cardinal arithmetic.

## Honest scope of the "super-Turing" claim

The results prove *oracle capacity*: once arbitrary history functionals are
admitted at limits, the fixed radius-one successor law hosts a faithful copy of
the entire Boolean predicate space. They do **not** claim Rule 110 manufactures
an undecidable predicate from computable data — `predicateLimit` receives `P` as
external data and need not be computable.

## Open directions

1. **Canonical limit rules.** Replace the scheduled `predicateLimit` by an
   intrinsic `liminf`/`limsup` convention on the cell history and characterise
   which predicates are then realisable. Conjecture: a computable limsup rule
   still exceeds ordinary Turing power (this is the "super-Turing from a
   computable convention" hypothesis, currently open).

2. **Infinite Time Turing Machines (ITTM).** Simulate an ITTM transition system
   block-for-block by `omegaSquaredRun`, then push to an instruction-level
   encoding. The abstract transition-system simulation is within reach; the
   machine encoding is the substantial open step.

3. **Ordinal universality of Rule 110.** Prove/refute that Rule 110 with a fixed
   canonical limit rule is universal for ordinal computation up to a specified
   ordinal height.

4. **Conservative finite embedding.** Formalise that every finite Rule 110
   computation embeds into an `ω²` run as block 0 (a `sorry`-free conservativity
   theorem), making the transfinite model a genuine extension.

5. **Higher ordinals.** Generalise from `ω²` to `ω^n` and `ω^ω` by iterating the
   two-layer construction, and relate the reachable predicate classes to the
   ordinal height (a hyperarithmetic/analytical-hierarchy connection).

6. **Cardinality sharpening.** Extend `continuum_scheduled_histories` to the full
   history space (arbitrary functionals, not just Boolean schedules) and locate
   its cardinality in the cardinal hierarchy.
